name: Pratt (Shelby) knot

card.summary: A symmetrical, medium-sized necktie knot that gives a neat triangle at the collar and suits shorter ties.
card.aka: Shelby knot; Pratt knot; Nicky knot (variant)

quick.overview:
The Pratt knot, also called the Shelby knot, is a way of tying a necktie that produces a symmetrical, medium-thick knot. It helps someone look polished in a shirt and tie: the even triangle sits neatly in the collar without the bulk of a full Windsor.

It is tied inside out and uses less of the tie's length than a Windsor or half-Windsor, which makes it useful for shorter ties or taller wearers. It was little known in fashion circles until a 1989 New York Times article drew attention to it.
quick.how: Tied with the tie's seam facing out at the start, it is often chosen for spread or medium collars. Style writers describe it as a step up in difficulty from the four-in-hand, with a more symmetrical result.
quick.risks: No health risks. A knot that is too large or tight for the collar can look cramped; ties made of thick fabric produce bulkier knots.

lead: The Pratt knot, also called the Shelby knot, is a way of tying a necktie that produces a medium-sized, symmetrical knot. It is tied inside out, with the seam of the tie facing outward at the start, and it ends in a compact, even triangle with a dimple under the knot. [1][7]

For appearance, the knot is chosen for what it does at the collar. Its symmetry reads as tidy and deliberate, it fills a spread or semi-spread collar without the bulk of a full Windsor, and it uses less tie length than the half-Windsor or Windsor, which suits shorter ties and taller wearers. [1][7] Style guides place it between the slim four-in-hand and the broader half-Windsor, so it is a way to get a balanced shirt-and-tie look from one tie. [3][4][7]

The knot's origin story is unusually well documented for a piece of menswear: a Washington lobbying-organisation employee named Jerry Pratt tied his ties this way for decades, a Minneapolis television anchor named Don Shelby learned it from him and wore it on air, and a 1989 New York Times article spread the story. [1][7] The Pratt knot is the non-self-releasing sibling of the Nicky knot. [6]

paras: The Pratt knot is a variation of the Nicky knot. Both are tied inside out, but only the Nicky is self-releasing. Unlike the four-in-hand, which Wikipedia calls notably asymmetric, the Pratt knot is symmetrical and of medium thickness. [1][4]

In the notation of The 85 Ways to Tie a Tie, the knot is written Lo Ci Lo Ri Co T and numbered knot 5. [1] The same notation gives the half-Windsor as knot 7, the four-in-hand as knot 2 and the Nicky as knot 4. [4][5][6]

Described in general terms, tying starts with the tie flipped so the seam faces out. The wide end is wrapped around the narrow end to make a horizontal band and a central loop, and the knot is then tightened and slid up to the collar with the dimple centred. [7] Because the first move is inverted, the finished knot shows the tie's face and an even crossover without needing much adjustment, and writers say it can often be tied without a mirror. [7]

Wikipedia describes the half-Windsor as larger than both the four-in-hand and the Pratt knot, and the full Windsor as wider still and bulkier. [4][5][3] The Pratt knot therefore occupies a middle position: broader and more balanced than the four-in-hand, but slimmer and lower than the half-Windsor. [4][7]
Grokipedia says the knot uses one wrap in front of the narrow end and one behind, forming two layers that spread tension evenly and give a mirrored crossover and compact triangular front view. [7]

Style guidance summarised on Grokipedia lists medium-spread, semi-spread, straight-point and wide-cutaway collars as good matches, and cautions that extremely narrow collars can show gaps if the knot is not tightened precisely. [7] It is described as working with most tie fabrics, including thicker ones. [7]

The Windsor knot is the knot most associated with very wide collars and bulky knots, and Wikipedia notes it is wider than most common knots and suits spread or cutaway collars. [3] Wikipedia's necktie article observes that knot choice is typically paired with the cut of the shirt collar. [2]

Because the Pratt knot consumes less of the tie than the half-Windsor or Windsor, it is recommended for shorter ties or taller wearers, where the tie's tip might otherwise fall short of the belt line. [1] The necktie article notes that tie length has shifted over the decades: interwar ties were shorter because trousers sat higher, and ties lengthened to about 57 inches in the 1990s as trousers moved to the hips. [2]

Jerry Pratt, an employee of the US Chamber of Commerce, created the knot in the late 1950s, according to Wikipedia. [1] Grokipedia says he used it exclusively for around 30 years, valuing a simple, balanced knot he could tie quickly without a mirror, and that the method remained personal and unpublished during that time. [7]

Grokipedia also reports that similar inverted-start methods were reportedly used by tailors in Milan in the 1920s and by Americans during World War II, which complicates a single-inventor account. [7] The Nicky knot, Pratt's self-releasing relative, is likewise described by Wikipedia as having originated in Milan. [6]

In 1986, when Pratt was 92 according to Wikipedia, he taught the knot to television reporter Don Shelby, whom he felt was tying his tie poorly on air. Shelby refined the method with Kingford Bavender, a local clothier, and wore it on air with a spread collar, where it drew notice for its symmetry and precision. This is why the knot is also called the Shelby knot. [1] Grokipedia places the encounter at the Minneapolis station WCCO-TV, and says Shelby and the clothier settled on a five-step method that prompted viewers to contact the station. [7] Grokipedia's own text dates the encounter inconsistently, giving both 1986 and 1989.

A New York Times article titled 'As Neckwear Goes, This Knot's News', published 30 August 1989, helped bring the knot to wider attention. Wikipedia reports that, according to that article, the knot had been unknown in the fashion world and was not recorded in the tie industry's standard reference of the time. [1] Wikipedia also cites coverage in People magazine and trade press about a Shelby-branded tie collection. [1]

Wikipedia's necktie article lists four main knots in rising order of difficulty: the four-in-hand, the Pratt (Shelby), the half-Windsor and the Windsor. [2] The four-in-hand became fashionable in Britain in the 1850s. [2] The Windsor is named for the Duke of Windsor, though Wikipedia says the Duke is more likely to have obtained his wide knots with thick ties and a four-in-hand than to have invented it. [2][3]

In the late 1990s Cambridge physicists Thomas Fink and Yong Mao used a mathematical model of tying moves to count 85 possible knots, and selected 13 as aesthetic on grounds of symmetry and balance, with three variants. The results were published for general readers as The 85 Ways to Tie a Tie. [2] Wikipedia's Pratt article uses that book's notation for the knot. [1]

Wikipedia also notes that the Pratt name is sometimes used loosely for the Nicky knot, which is tied the same way but self-releasing. [1][6] Other knots listed in the necktie article include the Atlantic, Prince Albert, Christensen, Trinity and Grantchester. [2]

The knot is an example of a tie technique that spread through broadcast exposure rather than through a tailor or manufacturer. According to Wikipedia, Shelby's on-air use was covered by People magazine and was followed by a Shelby-branded tie line produced with a St. Paul clothier. [1] Grokipedia reports coverage in the New York Times and The Daily Telegraph and calls it one of the few modern innovations in necktie knotting. [7]

Interest in knots such as the Pratt tends to appear in men's style and dress-code discussions, where the choice of knot is treated as one of the few adjustable parts of a suit-and-tie look. Wikipedia notes, for example, that the United States Army and Navy permit the four-in-hand, half-Windsor and Windsor for service neckties, a list that does not include the Pratt. [4]
Wearing a tie knot carries no health risk. Style writers note practical limits: a knot that is too large or tight for the collar can look cramped, and thick fabrics produce bulkier knots. [7]
No studies found. Research on tie knots in the literature is mathematical, such as the Fink and Mao enumeration of possible knots. [2]
